html:
The Normandy landings took place on 6 June 1944, known as D-Day, on the coast of Normandy in northern France. Troops of the United States, Britain and Canada came ashore against German defences in the largest invasion by sea in history.

Germany had held France since 1940. Stalin had long pressed his allies to open a second front in the west. The Allies, under the American general Dwight Eisenhower, gathered their forces in southern England. Fake armies and false radio traffic made the Germans expect the landing near Calais. In the night three airborne divisions dropped behind the coast. At dawn about 7,000 ships and boats put troops onto five beaches along 80 km of shore. At Omaha Beach the Americans were pinned down under the bluffs and lost over 2,000 men before breaking out. By night about 156,000 Allied soldiers were ashore. About 4,400 had been killed.

Weeks of hard fighting in the hedgerows followed, until the Allies broke out in late July and freed Paris on 25 August. Germany was now squeezed between the western Allies and the Soviet armies. It surrendered in May 1945, ending World War II in Europe.
